Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 9 periods = 360 minutes
Total: 9 periods · 6h 0min

periods.activity_title: First Reading — Meena, the Stream, and the Boats

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read + Let us think — A.1 (p.58): What was Meena playing with?

time_bands.activity: Teacher invites students to look at the chapter title and illustration. Students say what they see — a stream, a bridge, a child — before a word is read.
Teacher reads the story aloud from Textbook pp. 56–58, using a slightly different voice for Meena and the boy. Students listen with books open and follow along.
Shared re-reading: teacher and students read key dialogue passages together — Meena's angry shout and the boy's admission — chorally and with feeling.
Let us read + Let us think — A.1 ("What was Meena playing with?"): students answer orally in a full sentence; teacher accepts and repeats the answer clearly for the class.
Teacher briefly recaps: Meena, the stream, the paper boats, and a naughty boy. Students close books and whisper one thing they remember to a neighbour.

periods.teacher_notes: This is the students' first full encounter with the story, so pace the read-aloud slowly enough to let the illustrations guide meaning. The shift from Meena's anger to her generosity at the end often surprises students — pause there and let the silence land before moving on.

periods.activity_title: Comprehension Deep-Dive — Why Was Meena Angry?

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read + Let us think — A.2–3 (p.59): Why was Meena angry? How did she help the boy?
Let us read + Let us think — C.1–4 (p.59): True or False — boy's fun, Meena running home, boy's skill, colour of paper.

time_bands.activity: Teacher retells the story in three sentences, naming Meena, the stream, and the boy. Students raise a hand when they hear something they remember from the story.
Let us read + Let us think — A.2–3 ("Why was Meena angry? / How did Meena help?"): pairs discuss quietly, then individual students share answers aloud; teacher writes key phrases on the board.
Let us read + Let us think — C.1–4 ("True or False"): teacher reads each statement aloud; students show thumbs up or down, then justify in one sentence with the book open.
Class discusses: what changed in the boy's behaviour, and why? Teacher guides students to name patience and teaching as the reason peace returned to the stream.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often give C.2 (Meena ran home) as True because running away seems natural — prompt them to re-read Meena's words to the boy before confirming. Encourage answers in complete sentences throughout; single-word responses are gently expanded by the teacher.

periods.activity_title: Paper, Play, and Games — Small-Group Discussion

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think + Let us speak — B.1–2 (p.59): what can you make with paper? What games do you play?

time_bands.activity: Teacher models the discussion opener: "Meena made paper boats — I could also make a paper hat." Invites two or three students to add their own ideas before groups form.

Let us think + Let us speak — B.1 ("What else can you make with paper?"): students work in groups of four, each sharing at least one idea. Teacher circulates and prompts quieter students with: "Have you ever folded paper into anything?"

Let us think + Let us speak — B.2 ("What games do you play? Which do you like most? Why?"): each student tells the group one game and one reason. A group reporter shares the most popular game with the class.
Quick class round-up: teacher notes the games named on the board. Students observe that some games, like Meena's paper-boat play, need no equipment at all.

periods.teacher_notes: B.2 is richer when students give a reason, not just a name — keep nudging "Why do you like it?" to move beyond listing. Watch that group reporters do not simply list all answers; train them to say the group's agreed favourite with a reason.

periods.activity_title: Picture Story — Manish Saves the Ant

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak — picture series (p.60): tell the story of Manish saves the ant to the class.

time_bands.activity: Teacher walks the class through the six pictures on Textbook p. 60 one at a time — naming what is seen: Manish walking, the ant in water, the paper-boat raft, and the rescue. Students call out what they notice in each frame.
Teacher models a two-sentence retelling using pictures one and two: "Manish was walking by the stream. He saw a tiny ant struggling in the water." Students practise the same two sentences together.

Let us speak — picture story ("Tell the story of Manish saves the ant"): students work in pairs, each narrating the full six-picture sequence to their partner. Teacher listens in and offers a quiet prompt when a student is stuck.
Three volunteers tell the story to the whole class. After each retelling, classmates say one thing the speaker did well — a clear beginning, a describing word, a strong ending.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes tell only the rescue moment and skip the setup — encourage them to start from picture one so the story has a beginning, middle, and end. The connection between Manish using a paper boat as a raft and Meena's paper-boat play is worth naming: both stories show paper boats doing something kind.

periods.activity_title: Pronouns He and She — Replacing Names in Sentences

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn — A.1–4 (p.61): fill in blanks with 'he' or 'she' for Rani, Sahil, Durga, Ranjit.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes on the board: "Meena bent down. _____ launched a paper boat." Students decide which word fills the blank and explain why. Teacher introduces the term 'pronoun' simply: a word that stands in for a name.
Teacher reads the two model examples from Textbook p. 61 aloud — Meena → she, the boy → he. Students underline the original name and the pronoun that replaces it in each example.

Let us learn — A.1–4 ("Fill in the blanks with 'he' or 'she'"): students complete all four items independently in their notebooks. Teacher writes answer options prominently: 'he' and 'she'. Students check in pairs before the whole-class review.

Oral extension: teacher says a name — Anita, Ravi, Sunita, Mohan — and students call out "he" or "she" as fast as they can. Teacher returns to the story: "The boy gave Meena the boat. _____ was grateful." Students supply the pronoun.

periods.teacher_notes: The name Durga is sometimes assumed male by students unfamiliar with it — use the sentence context ("is going to school") rather than the name alone to model the decision. Avoid explaining the pronoun rule as an isolated grammar point; always tie back to the sentence pair from the story.

periods.activity_title: Prepositions in Context — Where Is Each Object?

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn — B.1–5 (p.62): choose on/under/in for bat, bag, ball, car, books using the bedroom picture.

time_bands.activity: Teacher places a book on the desk, under the chair, and inside a bag — pausing each time to ask "Where is the book now?" Students supply the preposition: on, under, in. Teacher writes the three words on the board.
Students open Textbook p. 62 and study the bedroom picture. Teacher guides a picture-walk: "Find the bat — where is it? Find the books — are they in, on, or under something?"

Let us learn — B.1–5 ("Choose on/under/in"): students write all five answers. Teacher reminds students that the picture is the evidence — not guesswork. Pairs compare answers before whole-class check.
Students write two original sentences using the bedroom picture — one with 'on' and one with 'under' or 'in' — about any objects they can see. Two volunteers read theirs aloud.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently confuse 'on' and 'in' for the chair and shelves — remind them that 'in' implies enclosed space and 'on' means resting on a surface. The sentence-writing extension at the close is brief by design; accept any grammatically correct use of the target preposition.
materials: A book and a bag (for the opening demonstration)

periods.activity_title: Picture Writing — A Day at the Park

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write — A (p.64): write a few lines about the park picture using the clue words.

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 64 and study the park picture together. Teacher names each element — slide, see-saw, swings, children — and writes the eight clue words on the board: park, children, playing, see-saw, swings, slide, enjoying, happy.

Teacher models aloud: "There is a park. Children are playing on the swings. They are happy." Students help add a sentence using 'see-saw'. The model shows three simple sentences using clue words — not a paragraph to copy.

Let us write — A ("Write a few lines about the park picture"): students write independently in their notebooks using the clue words. Teacher circulates, pointing at the picture when a student is stuck, and asking "What do you see here?"
Three students read their writing aloud. After each reading, teacher asks the class: "Did she use all the clue words? What describing word did he add?" Brief peer appreciation — one thing done well.

periods.teacher_notes: Some students copy the model sentences; gently redirect them to the picture and ask what they personally see. Clue words are a scaffold, not a formula — accepting sentences that use the clue words in a different order is correct practice.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us do — A (p.63): follow the six steps to draw a rangoli on the dot grid.
Let us explore — B (p.65): solve the toys-and-games crossword (Across and Down clues).

homework.task_brief: Let us explore — A (p.66): ask an elder at home about a game they played when young; be ready to share it.

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays Textbook p. 63 and walks through all six steps of the rangoli diagram, pointing to each one and naming the change — "Step 3 adds the diagonal lines." Students trace the progression with their finger.

Let us do — A ("Draw a rangoli following the six steps"): students use the blank dot-grid on p. 63 and replicate the pattern step by step. Teacher circulates and helps students who lose their place in the sequence.

Let us explore — B ("Solve the crossword"): students turn to p. 65 and work through the Across and Down clues on toys and games. Teacher reads each clue aloud once; students write answers in the grid.
Quick class check of crossword answers — teacher says the number and students call out the word. Homework task explained: talk to an elder at home and find out one game they played as a child.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who finish the rangoli quickly can colour it — this keeps them engaged while others complete the grid. For the crossword, reading the clue aloud and pausing before revealing the answer gives students a moment to retrieve the word independently.

periods.activity_title: Whole-Chapter Celebration — From Paper Boats to Paper Rangoli

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses a bridging question: "Meena resolved a quarrel by teaching the boy to make paper boats. Have you ever solved a problem by sharing a skill?" Students share briefly in pairs, then two or three speak to the class.

Pronoun and preposition rapid-fire review: teacher gives sentences from the story — "Meena placed the boats in the stream. _____ watched them sail." Students supply the pronoun and a preposition. Teacher writes correct answers on the board.

Students write three sentences in their notebooks: one about Meena using a pronoun correctly, one about where Manish found the ant using a preposition, and one about the park picture using a clue word. Teacher circulates and gives quick feedback.

Story retelling round: one student starts the story of Meena and the paper boats in one sentence; the next continues for one sentence; the class builds the story together until the ending. Teacher steps in only if the chain breaks.

Students who spoke to an elder at home share the game they discovered — a quick round of two or three sharings. Teacher names the theme that runs through the chapter: games, paper, kindness, and learning from each other.

periods.teacher_notes: The writing activity draws on the pronoun work from the story, the preposition work from the bedroom picture, and the clue-word writing from the park activity — it is a natural check of all three without being a formal test. Keep the tone celebratory and let the story retelling chain run with minimal correction.

items.source_context: Meena's paper-boat play, the boy's mischief, his admission, and her generous offer to teach.
items.item_stem:
Read the sentences below. Write TRUE or FALSE for each one.
1. The boy capsized Meena's boats because he wanted to be unkind to her forever.
2. The boy admitted he did not know how to make paper boats.
3. Meena refused to help the boy and walked home.
4. Meena brought coloured paper in different sizes to the stream.

options.text: Meena brought coloured paper in different sizes to the stream.
Meena refused to help the boy and walked home.
The boy admitted he did not know how to make paper boats.
The boy capsized Meena's boats because he wanted to be unkind to her forever.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1 — False (the boy said it was fun, not a desire to be permanently unkind). 2 — True (he admitted he wanted to play but could not make boats). 3 — False (Meena offered to help rather than leaving). 4 — True (she took out coloured paper in different sizes).

items.source_lo: Student retrieves explicit information and makes simple inferences using a narrative text as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Meena's paper-boat play, the boy's mischief, his admission, and her generous offer to teach.
items.item_stem: At the end of the story, both Meena and the boy gently place their boats in the stream and watch them sail together. What do you think changed between them from the beginning of the story to this moment? Write two or three sentences.

expected_elements: Names the conflict at the start (boy capsizing boats).
Notes the boy's admission and Meena's choice to teach.
Shows understanding that sharing turned conflict into friendship.

items.item_stem:
Look at the six pictures on Textbook page 60. Choose the correct answer.
What does Manish use to rescue the ant from the stream?

options.label: A
options.text: A leaf he finds on the ground

options.label: B
options.text: A paper boat he makes as a raft

options.label: C
options.text: A stick floating in the water

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student may have inferred a natural rescue tool without looking at the pictures carefully.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student recalled water and floating but confused the rescue object.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student imagined a direct physical rescue, missing the paper-boat detail in the pictures.

items.item_stem: Look at the six pictures on Textbook page 60 showing how Manish saves the ant. Tell the whole story to your teacher or a partner, starting from when Manish first sees the ant and ending when the ant is safely on land. Use at least four pictures in your telling.

expected_elements: Mentions Manish spotting the ant in water.
Describes the paper-boat raft saving the ant.
States the ant reaches safety at the end.

items.item_stem: Look at the picture on Textbook page 64. Choose the sentence that best describes what the children are doing in the park.

options.label: A
options.text: The children are eating their lunch under a tree in the park.

options.label: B
options.text: The children are flying kites in the park and a dog is chasing them.

options.label: C
options.text: The children are playing on the swings, see-saw, and slide and they look happy.

options.label: D
options.text: The children are sitting quietly and reading books in the park.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Student may not have looked at the picture carefully and defaulted to a classroom activity.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student recognised the park setting but invented an activity not shown in the picture.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student added details from imagination rather than reading the picture.

Fill in each blank with the correct word from the box. Each word may be used more than once.

Words: he   she   on   under   in

1. Meena took out coloured paper. ________ folded it carefully.
2. The boy watched Meena. ________ was surprised.
3. The paper boat sailed ________ the stream.
4. Meena kept the paper ________ her bag.
5. The boy sat ________ the bank of the stream.

Sentence to say: "The paper boat floated on the water."

expected_elements: Reads the given sentence clearly and correctly.
Written sentence uses 'under' to show position.

items.item_stem: Think about one game you know well — it could be a game you play at home, at school, or one you have heard about from an elder. Tell your teacher: what is the game called, how do you play it, and why do you enjoy it? Speak in three or four sentences.

expected_elements: Explains at least one rule or action in the game.
Gives a personal reason for enjoying it.
